summary: Discovery focused on incident tolerance, multi-region failover, and trade-offs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Cygnus is sensitive to p99 latency spikes and wants clear fallback rules that preserve availability while controlling cost. Security and auditability (KMS, audit logs, SSO) are gating factors for any Dedicated/Private pilot.
topics: fallback policies; multi-region routing; SLA expectations; canary/rollout behavior; KV/prefix cache; cold starts; model tiering and graceful degradation; security controls (KMS, SSO, audit logs); benchmarking plan
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-10 14:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Rivera (Redwood SE), Samir Joshi (CSM), Emma Li (CTO - Cygnus), Tariq Hassan (Head of ML), Priya Kumar (SRE Lead), Liam O'Connor (SecOps), Nina Park (Product PM)

Auto-summary: (auto-generated, rough) Cygnus wants to understand Redwood's strategies for keeping user-facing inference online during partial outages. They care about failover latency, whether traffic can be switched to cheaper model variants, and what guarantees Redwood provides for Dedicated vs Hosted. They've requested security docs and a short benchmark.

00:00 - Olivia Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you all making time. quick intro from our side - i'm olivia, account exec, and marco's our systems engineer who will walk through the technical options.
00:18 - Emma Li: thanks, olivia. quick context — we run conversational search across europe and NA, monthly heavy peaks, and we have strict uptime expectations for premium customers. we're evaluating whether we go Redwood Hosted first, or commit to Dedicated given our SLAs.
00:35 - Marco Rivera: great, can you give us the SLOs you're targeting, and what 'strict uptime' means in practice?
00:42 - Tariq Hassan: target is 99.95 for the product tier we care about, p99 under 600ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) and p50 under 120ms. also, we need clear behavior during regional outages — we want requests not to error out, even if latency increases.
01:05 - Priya Kumar: and from infra side, we require audit logs, KMS integration for key management, and the ability to route traffic through a VPC for the pilot.
01:20 - Olivia Chen: totally understood. quick high-level: Hosted can hit those SLOs for most workloads; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and more predictable p99 behavior. Private (VPC/on-prem) is the path for strict network controls and data residency. For incident tolerance we provide automated fallback policies — model degradation, region failover, and capacity-tier fallback.
01:50 - Liam O'Connor: can you explain 'model degradation' — do you mean switching to a smaller model automatically? what's the latency hit when that happens?
02:02 - Marco Rivera: yes, for example if the primary model is a 70B float-16 variant, we can route to a quantized 7B or 13B variant. the platform can do instant routing policy changes, though cold-start behavior depends on whether the fallback variant is warm in the cluster. if it's warm, the latency delta is usually +40-120ms; if cold, could be seconds.
02:30 - Emma Li: seconds is... risky. we need predictable behavior during failover windows. is there an option to keep fallbacks warm?
02:40 - Marco Rivera: yep — warm pools are supported in Dedicated and via pinning in Hosted reserved capacity; you can keep an idle allocation for standby variants. that does increase cost, obviously.
03:00 - Tariq Hassan: what's the typical cost multiplier to keep standby warm in Dedicated?
03:08 - Olivia Chen: it depends on instance size and how many regions. rough ballpark for a single standby GPU pool is ~0.25x to 0.5x of active cost if it's lightly provisioned; we'll run numbers in the pilot.
03:25 - Nina Park: when you say regions — do you support active-active multi-region model serving with sticky session routing? how do you handle session affinity for chat applications?
03:38 - Marco Rivera: yes, active-active is supported. session affinity is app-level — we can do routing headers and cookies to prefer origin region, but we also have last-kv-caching and prefix caches to reduce cross-region cold-start effects. the KV cache currently replicates metadata — but full KV replication across regions would add complexity and cost, so most customers accept eventual-miss behavior on cross-region failovers.
04:10 - Priya Kumar: that's important. our product can't tolerate token-loss or hallucination spikes after failover. do you have strategies to keep model outputs consistent — e.g., deterministic seeds, same model weights across regions?
04:22 - Marco Rivera: model weights are the same across regions for a given pinned version. randomness can be controlled by seeding where applicable. we also recommend ramped traffic shifts — a canary window to validate outputs before shifting 100% traffic.
04:40 - Emma Li: can you describe the canary workflow — say we have a region down, how quickly can you re-route and how does the canary run?
04:50 - Marco Rivera: our standard policy is configurable: immediate failover (fast path), staged canary (5-10% for 5-15 minutes) or manual approval. immediate failover trades validation for speed. staged canary gives you time to check for quality regressions.
05:15 - Tariq Hassan: quality regressions are my main worry — switching to smaller models might be cheaper but could degrade LLM-aware features like entity extraction. can we set guardrails that detect quality drift and automatically rollback?
05:28 - Marco Rivera: you can tie quality monitoring to an eval set; if metrics drop beyond a threshold, we'll auto-roll back or route to a fallback that prioritizes quality. Redwood Optimize also recommends quantization profiles per workload to preserve important ops.
05:48 - Olivia Chen: also to add — during pilot we'll instrument key prompts and set alerting for accuracy/regression so you don't get blind failovers.
06:00 - Priya Kumar: on the security side, how are audit logs surfaced? we need immutable logs of inference requests and admin actions for SOC2 audits.
06:08 - Samir Joshi: audit logs include model version changes, routing policy edits, and API tokens used. we can push logs to your SIEM via syslog or to an S3 bucket with object immutability.
06:28 - Liam O'Connor: do logs contain prompt text? that's sensitive — we need the ability to redact or not capture prompts, or to only store hashes.
06:36 - Samir Joshi: configurable. by default we log metadata (IDs, model, route changes). prompt capture is optional and can be redacted or STORED encrypted with your KMS. we support customer-managed keys so only you can decrypt prompts.
06:58 - Emma Li: good. circling back to SLAs — do you offer different uptime numbers for Hosted vs Dedicated?
07:08 - Olivia Chen: Hosted standard SLA is 99.9% for paid tiers; Dedicated has a stronger SLA option up to 99.95 or custom contractual SLAs depending on committed capacity and region coverage. Private/on-prem is negotiated as part of enterprise contract.
07:30 - Nina Park: what's the penalty or credit structure — i.e., how do you measure downtime for credits?
07:37 - Olivia Chen: we measure by route-level availability and p99 against configured SLO windows; credits are tiered based on the percent below SLA over monthly windows — we can share standard SLRs in the security pack.
07:52 - Tariq Hassan: performance during traffic spikes — do you autoscale, and how fast? we have 5-minute flash spikes regularly.
07:59 - Marco Rivera: autoscaling is workload-aware with continuous batching; for short spikes, we rely on queueing and burst capacity. Dedicated can reserve burst capacity and hot-standby instances for sub-1m scale-up. cold-start for new containers or quantized variants is the bigger factor.
08:25 - Priya Kumar: we need a runbook for outage scenarios — if a zone goes down in eu-west, show our SREs the exact steps: how traffic is shifted, expected latency increases, and when to flip to manual. do you provide playbooks?
08:36 - Samir Joshi: yes, we provide operational playbooks per customer and can include exact CLI commands and console steps. we can also coordinate runbook drills during the pilot.
08:50 - Emma Li: during incidents, who drives the mitigation? our SREs or Redwood?
08:56 - Olivia Chen: it can be collaborative. for Hosted we typically do joint mitigation — Redwood ops will suggest routing changes; for Dedicated you can opt for self-serve controls with ops support. we'll clarify in the SOW.
09:12 - Nate (customer, off-mic) [mislabelled speaker in transcript]
09:20 - Marco Rivera: small note — sometimes the transcript auto-labels a speaker weirdly, ignore that. back to architecture — many customers use a hybrid: Hosted in primary region with Dedicated standby in a second region for critical traffic.
09:40 - Tariq Hassan: hybrid is interesting — does that complicate data handling? we have EU data residency obligations for some projects.
09:48 - Marco Rivera: you can configure routing by tenant or dataset — EU tenants can be pinned to EU regions and audit logs stored to an EU S3 bucket with EU KMS. Private deployments can be used if you need on-prem for regulated workloads.
10:05 - Priya Kumar: for multi-region KV/cache replication — you said there are cost and consistency tradeoffs. can you quantify eventual consistency window?
10:16 - Marco Rivera: typical eventual replication for prefix cache is under 30s for most ops, but worst-case cross-region replication could be minutes under heavy load. that's why many customers avoid full-state replication and instead accept some cold misses post-failover.
10:38 - Emma Li: we have a feature that heavily depends on context carryover between turns — cold misses would break UX. could we implement sticky routing to avoid cross-region misses for active sessions?
10:50 - Marco Rivera: yes, sticky routing is the recommended pattern for that feature. it preserves the KV/Prefix cache locality until a TTL expires or explicit session transfer is invoked.
11:05 - Nina Park: what's the simplest fallback topology you'd recommend for a pilot: minimal cost but safe availability?
11:12 - Marco Rivera: simple pattern: primary Hosted region with a standby model variant warmed in same region; a second region with cold standby for disaster; auto-redirect with staged canary. That keeps cost low while providing an escape hatch.
11:32 - Tariq Hassan: i'd rather test cost/latency of two options: warm fallback in same region vs active-active across two regions. can we get a cost delta?
11:40 - Olivia Chen: yes, SE will model both during the benchmarking run.
11:45 - Priya Kumar: logging and telemetry — can you expose token-level latency and per-route error rates to our Grafana?
11:53 - Samir Joshi: yes, we export metrics via Prometheus endpoints, and can set up dashboards in Grafana or push to cloud monitoring.
12:05 - Liam O'Connor: does Redwood support RBAC at a fine granularity? e.g., allow only our secops to change routing policies, but not developers?
12:12 - Marco Rivera: yes, RBAC and SSO/SAML are supported. we integrate with IdP, and policies can be scoped to teams or roles.
12:25 - Emma Li: can we see an example of a routing policy JSON? would like to see the syntax — priority, conditions, model weights, canary windows.
12:34 - Marco Rivera: i'll attach examples in the follow-up. they look like simple rules: match conditions, percent traffic, target model, warm preference, timeout thresholds.
12:48 - Nina Park: failure modes — what happens if the routing control plane itself is degraded? do you have self-healing?
12:58 - Marco Rivera: control plane redundancy is multi-AZ; for Dedicated we can provide a private control plane option. the runtime nodes are independent and will accept local overrides; in the worst case we fall back to last-known routing policy until control plane is available.
13:22 - Tariq Hassan: what's the maximum supported model latency for bursty workloads before you recommend batching changes?
13:30 - Marco Rivera: continuous batching is tuned per workload; for real-time chat we tune batch latency targets below 30ms per-token added to p99. If you see model latencies exceed acceptable thresholds, we reduce batch window or move to higher capability instances.
13:50 - Olivia Chen: quick checkpoint — sounds like the three primary things: 1) you need warm fallback behavior and cost estimates, 2) security and auditability are blocking, 3) you want a benchmarking run with your prompt set. are we aligned?
14:03 - Emma Li: yes. plus a template playbook for our SREs.
14:10 - Marco Rivera: will do. more questions?
14:18 - Priya Kumar: micro-level — do you allow per-tenant routing policies? we'd like different fallback behavior for enterprise vs free tier customers.
14:27 - Marco Rivera: yes, policy scoping by tenant, route, or API key is supported.
14:33 - Tariq Hassan: let's talk about fail-open vs fail-closed — in some scenarios we'd rather degrade to a stub response than return an error. do you support structured fallback responses?
14:44 - Marco Rivera: yes, you can configure structured fallbacks: canned text, last-successful-response, or a deterministic small-model reply. many customers push last-successful-response for caching-friendly flows.
14:58 - Emma Li: does the platform support tool-calling or function calling, and how does that interact with fallbacks? if you have external tools that fetch user data, failures could cascade.
15:10 - Marco Rivera: function calling is supported. for fallbacks you can configure safe-stubs for tool outputs (e.g., cached or masked data) and set timeouts per tool to avoid cascading failures.
15:28 - Nina Park: onboarding timeline — if we decide to pilot, how long to stand up a Hosted pilot versus Dedicated?
15:35 - Olivia Chen: Hosted pilot can be set up in days (1-3) with shipping SDKs and dashboards. Dedicated is more like 4-8 weeks for reserved capacity provisioning and network setup, depending on regions. Private/on-prem takes longer.
15:52 - Priya Kumar: for Dedicated, what are the network requirements — do you provide peering, and can we put it behind our NGFW?
15:59 - Marco Rivera: yes, we support cloud peering, Direct Connect equivalents, and customer-managed ingress via NATs. Private deployment can be put entirely behind your NGFW.
16:14 - Tariq Hassan: curious about model version pinning and rollbacks — if we pin a version and later a bug is found, how fast can you roll forward/back?
16:25 - Marco Rivera: rollouts are orchestrated; you can do instant global rollback of routes, or a canary-based forward. rollback propagation is typically within seconds to a minute depending on topology.
16:40 - Emma Li: any documented incidents of significant cross-region failovers we can review for post-mortem best practices?
16:49 - Samir Joshi: yes, we'll include anonymized post-mortems and a couple runbooks that show the timeline and decisions — good learnings on how customers structured their canaries and warm pools.
17:05 - Nina Park: do you have any cost-saving recommendations we should consider for long-term — like model quantization vs larger batches?
17:13 - Marco Rivera: Redwood Optimize recommends workload-based quantization and school of batching; for interactive chat, quantization to int8 with selective operator preservation gives most wins. we can run an eval to estimate QoE impact.
17:30 - Priya Kumar: is there a way to throttle enterprise traffic differently during incidents to preserve 99.95 for premium customers?
17:39 - Marco Rivera: yes, traffic shaping and priority queues are supported so you can preserve capacity for high-tier customers during overloads.
17:50 - Emma Li: what kind of telemetry do you retain for debugging? we need traces, logs, and token-level timings for 30 days for investigations.
17:59 - Samir Joshi: standard retention is 30 days for telemetry in Hosted; extended retention is an add-on. logs can be exported to your retention store.
18:15 - Olivia Chen: quick recap of ask items: security docs, routing policy examples, fallback topologies + cost modeling, and a benchmark run. we'll follow up with calendar invites.
18:28 - Nina Park: can you also include an example SLO contract for 99.95 and what contractual credits look like?
18:36 - Olivia Chen: yes, will include sample SLO text.
18:40 - Tariq Hassan: one last technical quickie — how do you detect degradation? is it purely latency/error thresholds or model-level metrics?
18:47 - Marco Rivera: detection uses a combination: latency, error rates, and quality signals from profiles — you can feed custom eval metrics as well.
18:58 - Emma Li: thanks. next step — we'll pull together our prompt set and traffic shape and share by Friday.
19:06 - Olivia Chen: perfect. we'll get the security pack out, and marco will run the benchmark plan. thanks all.

(End of recording — remainder is Q&A and soft talk)
